## Important comparability caveats

**1. No unit-cost (CASM) data is available in these filings.** The industry-standard efficiency metric is cost per available seat mile (CASM, and CASM ex-fuel), which requires ASM capacity data. The source excerpt contains only revenue, fuel, labor, and operating income [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt — "Selected figures from each company's fiscal year 2024 Form 10-K (all calendar-year, Jan 1 – Dec 31; $ in millions; source: SEC XBRL financial data)"]. My analysis therefore uses **revenue-normalized cost ratios**, which conflate cost efficiency with pricing power (premium/loyalty revenue mix flatters Delta and United on this basis).

**2. Fiscal periods are aligned** — all five are calendar-year Jan 1–Dec 31 filers, so there is no fiscal-year mismatch [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

**3. Entity-level comparability is imperfect.** Alaska Air Group's FY2024 reflects a partial year of the Hawaiian Airlines acquisition (closed Sept 2024), so its full-year figures are not a clean run-rate. Delta, United, and American are holding companies consolidating large regional/subsidiary operations; Southwest is a single mainline carrier with no regional feed — a structurally different cost base.

## Derived metrics (implied opex = revenue − operating income)

| Airline | Revenue | Implied Opex | Opex/Rev | Op. Margin | Fuel % Rev | Labor % Rev |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Delta** | $61,643M | $55,648M | **90.3%** | **9.73%** | 17.1% | 26.2% |
| United | $57,063M | $51,967M | 91.1% | 8.93% | 20.6% | 29.2% |
| Alaska | $11,735M | $11,165M | 95.1% | 4.86% | 21.4% | 30.6% |
| American | $54,211M | $51,597M | 95.2% | 4.82% | 21.1% | 29.6% |
| Southwest | $27,483M | $27,162M | 98.8% | 1.17% | 21.2% | 44.5% |

Source figures: Delta $61,643M revenue / $10,566M fuel / $16,161M labor / $5,995M operating income; United $57,063M / $11,756M / $16,678M / $5,096M; Southwest $27,483M / $5,812M / $12,240M / $321M; American $54,211M / $11,418M / $16,021M / $2,614M; Alaska $11,735M / $2,506M / $3,588M / $570M [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt].

## Interpretation

**Delta** is the leader on every available measure: the lowest cost-to-revenue ratio (90.3%), the highest operating margin (9.73%), the lowest fuel intensity (17.1% of revenue — helped by its Trainer refinery, a structural advantage peers lack), and the lowest labor intensity (26.2%). United is a close second (91.1% opex/revenue).

**Southwest is the clear laggard**, converting only 1.2 cents of each revenue dollar to operating profit, with labor alone consuming 44.5% of revenue — roughly 15–18 points worse than the network carriers [DOC: airlines_costs_fy2024.txt: Southwest labor $12,240M on $27,483M revenue]. This inverts the historical low-cost-carrier narrative.

Caveat worth restating: Delta's advantage here is partly a *revenue* story (premium cabin and AmEx loyalty income inflate the denominator). On a true CASM basis Southwest would likely rank better than this table implies, and Delta worse — but that data is not in the source filings.

ANSWER: Delta Air Lines — lowest operating-expense-to-revenue ratio (90.3%), highest operating margin (9.73%), and lowest fuel (17.1%) and labor (26.2%) intensity of the five in FY2024. (Caveat: based on revenue-normalized cost ratios, not CASM, which is unavailable in the source filings; Alaska's FY2024 also includes only a partial year of Hawaiian.)
